signals.source_text: 🛩️ 𝑹𝒆𝒂𝒍-𝑻𝒊𝒎𝒆 3𝑫 𝑰𝑴𝑼 𝑴𝒐𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏 𝑽𝒊𝒔𝒖𝒂𝒍𝒊𝒛𝒆𝒓 𝒖𝒔𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝑹𝑶𝑺 2 𝑱𝒂𝒛𝒛𝒚, 𝑬𝑺𝑷32-𝑺3 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝑹𝑽𝒊𝒛2 Excited to share my latest project: a real-time 3D Flight Telemetry & IMU Visualizer tracking an F-15C Eagle model using an 𝐌𝐏𝐔𝟔𝟎𝟓𝟎 𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐫, custom ESP32-S3 firmware, and ROS 2 Jazzy! 💡 Engineering Highlights: 🔹 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐦𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 (𝐄𝐒𝐏-𝐈𝐃𝐅 𝐯𝟔.𝟎.𝟐): High-speed 𝟏𝟎𝟎 𝐇𝐳 CSV telemetry over 𝐔𝐒𝐁-𝐂𝐃𝐂 @ 𝟏𝟏𝟓𝟐𝟎𝟎 𝐛𝐚𝐮𝐝 with error-recovery mechanisms. 🔹 𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝐃𝐒𝐏): Implemented an automated 200-sample sensor offset calibration algorithm paired with a 𝟐𝐧𝐝-𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐮𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐒𝐎𝐒 𝐋𝐨𝐰-𝐏𝐚𝐬𝐬 𝐅𝐢𝐥𝐭𝐞𝐫 (𝐟𝐜=𝟐.𝟎 𝐇𝐳) to eliminate high-frequency mechanical noise. 🔹 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐫 𝐅𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: Utilized the 𝐢𝐦𝐮_𝐟𝐢𝐥𝐭𝐞𝐫_𝐦𝐚𝐝𝐠𝐰𝐢𝐜𝐤 𝐀𝐇𝐑𝐒 𝐚𝐥𝐠𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐦 to compute drift-free orientation quaternions (/imu/filtered). 🔹𝐑𝐎𝐒 𝟐 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞: Custom Python driver node, dynamic 𝐓𝐅𝟐 broadcaster (odom ➔ base_link), URDF model with mesh texturing, and live 6-DoF visualization in RViz2. 🔹 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐲 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲: Recorded telemetry via 𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐛𝐚𝐠𝟐 for data analysis and offline flight simulation. 💻 𝐓𝐞𝐜𝐡 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐜𝐤: 𝐑𝐎𝐒 𝟐 𝐉𝐚𝐳𝐳𝐲, 𝐔𝐛𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐮 𝟐𝟒.𝟎𝟒 𝐋𝐓𝐒, 𝐄𝐒𝐏-𝐈𝐃𝐅 (𝐂), 𝐏𝐲𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐧 (𝐍𝐮𝐦𝐏𝐲/𝐒𝐜𝐢𝐏𝐲), 𝐓𝐅𝟐, 𝐑𝐕𝐢𝐳𝟐. 📁 Check out the complete source code and technical handbook on GitHub: https://lnkd.in/dsDg39yv Special thanks to the #ROS and open-source robotics community! #Robotics #ROS2 #EmbeddedSystems #ESP32 #SensorFusion #SignalProcessing #RViz2 #AutonomousSystems #Engineering #Python #Cplusplus #C #TF2 #Madgwickfilter #MPU6050

These areas closely match the profile's focus on GNC, UAVs, autopilot algorithms, simulation, autonomy, telemetry, and control systems. signals.source_text: The drone now follows me completely autonomously. No GPS, no pilot. 🛸 A few months ago, I shared how I got this custom built quadcopter to hold a rock-solid hover indoors using just LiDAR and optical flow. That was the foundation. Now, the full autonomy stack is live. I’ve built a complete sim-to-real pipeline. The exact same ROS 2 stack that I developed and validated in a Gazebo Harmonic digital twin now flies the real aircraft. Here is what is happening under the hood on the onboard Raspberry Pi 4: - Perception: A live camera feed runs through MediaPipe Pose to extract shoulder landmarks and track the target. - Estimation: A pinhole camera model converts pixel measurements into a metric distance estimate and yaw error. - Control: A custom ROS 2 follow-controller calculates and streams velocity commands to the ArduPilot flight controller via MAVROS. - Fail-safe by design: If any node crashes or the target is lost, the system instantly degrades the aircraft into a safe, altitude-holding hover. The biggest engineering hurdle: Latency. Initially, the drone felt sluggish and overshot turns. Profiling the pipeline revealed the data was almost a second old. By switching QoS to BEST_EFFORT, enforcing latest-frame-only threading, and tuning the EMA filter, I cut the end-to-end latency down to ~240 ms. Now, it tracks where you are, not where you were. I am currently exploring Master's thesis and internship opportunities in Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) for Spring 2027. If your team is tackling similar autonomous challenges, I’d love to connect! For those of you building autonomous systems: what is the most stubborn sim-to-real gap you've ever had to bridge? 👇 #Robotics #ROS2 #AutonomousSystems #ComputerVision #Drones #EmbeddedSystems

signals.source_text: The EV didn't make NVH easier. It pushed the noise higher. Motor whine past 5 kHz. Gear mesh. Inverter harmonics. Road noise now the loudest source in the cabin. The Engineer's Guide to Modern NVH Simulation shows how to work the full range in MSC Nastran and Actran: heavy-fluid coupling, Virtual SEA, and ODYSSEE ROMs. Preview the first pages, then download the full guide below 👇

signals.source_text: When you work at a company building electric air taxis, it is easy to get ahead of yourself telling the story. At Joby Aviation , the future doesn't just happen on the flight line, it takes shape in the narrative we build around it. Spending my time interning with the MarComms team taught me that bringing quiet, zero-emissions flight to the world requires a special kind of bridge, one built out of pixels, story arcs, and authenticity. There’s a clear line between the hardware of aerospace and the "software" of brand building. On one side, you have revolutionary aircraft designed to fundamentally change how cities move. On the other, you have the daily rhythm of digital engagement: writing captions, analyzing audience sentiment, cutting video clips, and finding the exact angle that makes complex technology feel relatable on a smartphone screen. Crafting that bridge taught me a few core lessons about digital storytelling in a revolutionary industry: - Translation over declaration: Highlighting eVTOL specs is easy; making a transformed morning commute feel real to someone on their phone takes translation. - Authenticity anchors trust: When your product sounds like science fiction, hyper-polished PR can feel distant. The raw, human moments behind the tech always resonated most. - Audiences are co-pilots: In an emergent industry like eVTOL, every comment and question builds public trust in real time. Listening is just as vital as broadcasting. Leaving this internship, I’m deeply grateful to the incredible MarComms team at Joby who trusted me to help tell this story. A huge, special shout-out to Max Goldstein for pushing me past my comfort zone every day and showing me how to take complex engineering and give it the sizzle it deserves. Shaping the conversation around the future of flight has been an unforgettable experience, and I'm walking away with a completely reshaped toolkit, invaluable lessons, and a deep appreciation for this team. #JobyAviation #FutureOfFlight #DigitalMarketing #InternshipExperience #SantaCruz #Aviation #Storytelling

signals.why_relevant: технологии: autonomy; домены: defense; совпадение с профилем: autonomy.
signals.source_text: During a technical review, I asked to see the training data and validation methodology behind a company's "AI-based multi-sensor classifier." What I got back was a fixed decision tree with manually tuned thresholds — no train/test split, no retraining pipeline, a "confidence score" that was really just a normalized distance metric with no calibration behind it. Here's the part people miss: that's not automatically a bad system. A deterministic, explainable rule-based classifier can be exactly the right architectural choice for a safety-critical decision path — arguably safer than a black-box model in a domain where you'll eventually have to explain your logic to a test pilot or an OT&E board. The actual problem was calling it "AI." That label invites the wrong due-diligence questions — where's your training data, how do you retrain, what's your drift monitoring — and forfeits the credit you'd get for being deterministic and auditable in a domain where explainability is a selling point, not a weakness. How you characterize your own architecture changes which questions you get asked. Answer the right ones on your own terms. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #AI

signals.source_text: 𝗚𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻. 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺. 𝗧𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜. The semiconductor industry sits where all of these intersect. For decades it competed on efficiency and won. But efficiency alone no longer protects you when disruption stops being the exception and becomes the operating environment. In my conversations with semiconductor executives this past year, resilience comes up in every boardroom, but almost always framed as a supply chain problem. That instinct is right, but I've come to think it's too narrow. The more useful question isn't "How resilient is our supply chain?" It's "How resilient is our enterprise?" In my latest article, I explore why resilience must extend beyond the supply chain and begin with three critical questions every semiconductor leader should be asking.
